questions.question: In the full-stack mental model from the restaurant analogy, which part is responsible for storing your habits long-term?
options: The frontend (the dining room)
The API (the waiter)
The database (the walk-in fridge)
The browser's localStorage
questions.explanation: The database is the walk-in fridge where data is stored permanently; the frontend just displays things and the API just shuttles requests back and forth.

questions.question: What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?
options: A primary key links two tables; a foreign key uniquely identifies a row in its own table
A primary key uniquely identifies a row within its own table; a foreign key holds the primary key of a row in another table
They are two names for the same column
A primary key is always text; a foreign key is always a number
questions.explanation: A primary key (e.g. habits.id) uniquely identifies a row within its own table, while a foreign key (e.g. habits.user_id) holds the primary key of a row in another table, creating a link between them.

questions.question: When wiring up the Supabase client in your frontend, which key do you use, and what is the current name for it?
options: The publishable key (older projects call it the anon key) — it is safe to ship publicly
The service_role key — it bypasses all security
The publishable key — it must be kept secret in a backend
The anon key — newer projects renamed it the service_role key
questions.explanation: The public publishable key (labeled anon in older projects) is meant to be public and safe to ship in the frontend; what keeps data private is Row Level Security, and the service_role/secret key must never go in frontend code.

questions.question: After running an insert with the Supabase client, how do you know whether it actually worked?
options: Wrap it in try/catch — Supabase throws on failure
Check the returned error from the destructured { data, error }; success means error is null
Check the HTTP status code manually
A successful insert always returns true
questions.explanation: Supabase does not throw on a failed request — every call returns { data, error }, so you check error yourself, and a successful insert has error === null.

questions.question: Why is calling .delete() or .update() without an .eq() filter a dangerous common mistake?
options: It throws a syntax error and the call fails
It only ever affects the first row in the table
With no filter the operation hits every row your permissions allow
Supabase silently ignores filterless writes
questions.explanation: Without a filter, the update or delete hits every row your permissions allow, so you should always filter to the exact id with .eq('id', ...).

questions.question: What is a session, and what does the supabase-js client do with it on each request?
options: A copy of the database that the client caches locally and syncs on each request
A token proving the user is logged in; the client stores it and attaches it to every database request
The user_id column value, which the client writes into every new row
A password the client re-sends with each request to re-authenticate
questions.explanation: A session is a token proving the user is logged in; the supabase-js client stores it and attaches it to every database request so the backend knows who is asking.

questions.question: You enabled RLS and now every select returns an empty array with no error. What is almost certainly wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Your CRUD code is broken; rewrite the select query
RLS is on but you have no policies, so the table is locked; add policies scoped with auth.uid() = user_id
RLS is on and blocking you; the fix is to disable RLS
Your publishable key is wrong; swap in the service_role key
questions.explanation: Enabling RLS locks the table by default, so with no policies it correctly returns nothing; the fix is to add policies (e.g. using (auth.uid() = user_id)), never to disable RLS.

questions.question: Why does every Supabase call need a loading state when a useState update does not?
options: Supabase calls are slower only because of React re-renders
useState updates are async too, but Supabase disables them
Supabase calls are network requests over the internet that take real time and can fail, while a useState update is instant and local
Supabase requires a loading state for every call by API rule
questions.explanation: Supabase calls are network requests that go over the internet — they take real time and can fail — whereas a useState update is instant and local to the browser, which is why only the former needs loading and error states.
